points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: The role of Standard English in informal texts
points.detail: How SAE functions as the reference point that informality is measured against, and what it means for a text to depart from it deliberately rather than through error.

questions.q: Explain why a text can depart from Standard English deliberately rather than through error, and describe how you would tell the two apart in an informal text.
answer: Standard English is the codified variety used as a reference point, not a measure of correctness.
Deliberate departure is systematic and serves a purpose — solidarity, identity, humour, speed.
Error is inconsistent and serves no communicative function.
Consistency across the text, and whether the feature fits the tenor and audience, distinguish them.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Functions of language in a given context
points.detail: Jakobson's six functions — referential, emotive, conative, phatic, metalinguistic, poetic — and identifying which are operating in a text, usually more than one.

questions.q: A friend texts: 'hey u free sat? think im gonna lose it if i dont get out of the house lol'. Identify two functions of language operating and justify each.
answer: Referential — the message conveys information and a question about Saturday availability.
Emotive — 'lose it', 'lol' express the speaker's emotional state.
Also acceptable: phatic, maintaining the social connection between friends.
Conative if the request is read as directing the friend to respond.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Register, tenor and audience in informal texts
points.detail: How the relationship between participants, their social distance and the assumed audience drive the level of informality.

questions.q: Explain how tenor shapes the level of informality, using the contrast between a message to a sibling and one to a new employer.
answer: Tenor is the relationship between participants, including social distance and relative power.
Low social distance and equal power with a sibling permit slang, ellipsis and minimal mitigation.
High social distance and unequal power with an employer require standard forms, full clauses and negative politeness.
The same speaker shifts register because the tenor changes, not their ability.

points.title: Features of informal writing
points.detail: Across a range of texts: abbreviations, spellings reflecting pronunciation, syntactic creativity, ellipsis, shortened lexical forms, non-linear structure.

questions.q: Identify four features that mark a written text as informal and explain what each contributes to the relationship between writer and reader.
answer: Contractions and shortenings — signal casualness and speed.
Colloquial lexis or slang — signals shared identity and reduces social distance.
Ellipsis and sentence fragments — assume shared context between writer and reader.
Non-standard orthography, emojis, lower case — substitute for prosody and mark intimacy.
Each should be tied to intimacy, solidarity or equality.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Features of informal speech
points.detail: Spontaneity and planning both playing a role, prosodic and paralinguistic support, and the idiosyncratic choices individual speakers make.

questions.q: Explain why non-fluency features in a transcript are evidence of informality rather than evidence of a poor speaker.
answer: Spontaneous speech is planned in real time, so pauses, false starts and repairs are expected.
Their presence shows low planning and an unrehearsed exchange, characteristic of informal contexts.
Filled pauses also hold the floor while the speaker formulates the next utterance.
Judging them as errors is a prescriptivist reading; descriptively they are normal features of speech.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Context and language features in informal texts
points.detail: The relationship between the situational and cultural context of an exchange and the specific features that appear in it — the heart of every analytical commentary.

questions.q: Explain how the situational context of a group chat between close friends produces the specific language features found in it.
answer: Tenor: close, equal relationships mean low social distance and minimal face mitigation.
Field: everyday personal subject matter allows colloquial lexis rather than specialised terms.
Mode: written but spontaneous, so it borrows spoken features — ellipsis, fragments, emojis for prosody.
Shared cultural context means much can be left implicit, producing high inference and in-group references.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Features of spoken discourse in informal texts
points.detail: Openings and closings, adjacency pairs, minimal responses, overlapping speech, discourse markers and non-fluency features, and what each contributes.

questions.q: Explain how openings and closings differ between an informal conversation between friends and a formal job interview.
answer: Informal: openings are loose, may skip greetings entirely, and closings are negotiated over several turns.
Formal: openings follow convention with explicit greetings and often self-identification.
Formal closings are managed by the participant with higher status, signalling the end clearly.
The difference reflects tenor — social distance requires more explicit structuring.

points.title: Subsystem patterning, colloquial language and slang
points.detail: Identifying patterning across the subsystems, and the role of colloquialisms and slang in marking informality and in-group membership.

questions.q: Distinguish colloquial language from slang, and explain how each contributes to informality in a text between teenagers.
answer: Colloquial language is informal but widely understood across the speech community.
Slang is group-specific, changes faster, and marks membership of a particular group.
Colloquialism lowers formality and signals a relaxed register.
Slang additionally excludes outsiders and constructs in-group identity for the participants.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Taboo language, dysphemism and swearing
points.detail: Swearing patterns and taboo language as markers of informality and solidarity, and the social work they do beyond giving offence.

questions.q: A transcript of close friends contains repeated swearing. Explain why this is not necessarily aggressive, and identify what it is likely achieving.
answer: Swearing is not only used to offend — its function depends on context and tenor.
Among close friends it commonly signals solidarity and in-group membership.
It marks the exchange as informal and relaxed, where taboo constraints can be suspended.
It can also intensify emotion or add humour rather than express hostility.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Emoticons, emojis and context-specific graphemes
points.detail: How written informal texts substitute for prosody and paralinguistics, and how a grapheme's meaning shifts with context.

questions.q: Explain how emojis and non-standard orthography compensate for the absence of prosodic and paralinguistic features in written informal texts.
answer: Written text lacks pitch, stress, volume and facial expression, which carry attitude in speech.
Emojis substitute for facial expression, marking humour, sarcasm or softening a face-threatening act.
Capitals and repeated letters substitute for volume and elongation ('STOP', 'nooooo').
Meaning is context-specific and varies between groups and generations.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Discourse strategies and cooperation
points.detail: Topic management, turn-taking, repair sequences, and the ways speakers cooperate to keep an interaction running.

questions.q: Using the concepts of turn-taking, topic management and repair, explain how participants in an informal conversation cooperate.
answer: Turn-taking: participants use prosodic and grammatical cues to pass the floor; overlap is often supportive.
Topic management: topics are introduced, developed and shifted collaboratively rather than controlled by one speaker.
Repair: self-repair and other-repair fix breakdowns without threatening face.
Backchannels signal continued attention, encouraging the speaker to continue.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Informality for intimacy, solidarity and equality
points.detail: How informal choices reduce social distance, including the politeness strategies that support it.

questions.q: Explain how informal language can be used to build solidarity, and identify two specific features that achieve this.
answer: Solidarity is the sense of shared identity and belonging between participants.
Feature: slang or in-group lexis, comprehensible only to members, marking who belongs.
Feature: hypocoristics and nicknames, signalling familiarity and reducing social distance.
Also acceptable: swearing used non-aggressively, ellipsis assuming shared knowledge, positive politeness.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 1: Informality
points.title: Informality for innovation, harmony and in-group membership
points.detail: Promoting linguistic innovation, negotiating social taboos, building rapport, and signalling who belongs to the group and who doesn't.

questions.q: Explain how informal language promotes linguistic innovation and helps negotiate social taboos, giving an example of each.
answer: Informal contexts tolerate novelty, so neologisms, blends and new slang emerge and spread there first.
Example: internet-origin coinages entering everyday speech before any dictionary records them.
Taboo topics are negotiated through euphemism, dysphemism and humour, letting participants discuss the difficult.
Example: joking dysphemism about illness or death, which manages discomfort while allowing the subject to be raised.

points.title: Cohesion and coherence in informal texts
points.detail: The discourse factors that hold an informal text together, and why a text can be cohesive without being coherent or the reverse.

questions.q: Explain why an informal conversation between close friends may have low cohesion but remain highly coherent for its participants.
answer: Shared context means much is left implicit — ellipsis, deixis and unexplained references reduce surface cohesion.
Participants supply the missing links through inference from shared knowledge.
Coherence depends on whether it makes sense to its audience, not on explicit linking devices.
An outsider reading the same transcript may find it incoherent.

points.title: Transcription conventions
points.detail: The conventions for transcribing spoken English — symbols, legend and line numbers — and referring to line numbers accurately in an analysis.

questions.q: A transcript line reads: '12 A: so (.) i mean it's not [that] bad'. Explain what each convention represents.
answer: '12' is the line number, used for accurate reference in an analysis.
'(.)' marks a micropause — a brief pause too short to time.
'[' marks the onset of overlapping speech with another speaker.
Always quote line numbers when referring to a transcript in your answer.

points.area: Unit 3: Language variation and purpose — AoS 2: Formality
points.title: The role of Standard English in formal texts
points.detail: How SAE carries prestige in formal contexts, and what its use signals about the writer or speaker.

questions.q: Explain what a writer's use of Standard English in a formal text signals to the reader, and why the variety carries that force.
answer: It signals authority, credibility and membership of educated institutional discourse.
SAE carries overt prestige because it is the codified variety used by powerful institutions.
That prestige is a social fact, not a linguistic one — SAE is not inherently clearer or more logical.
Departing from it in a formal text risks the writer being judged as less competent.

Referential support: statistics or medical information establish the basis for the instruction.

questions.q: Explain how anticipating an unknown, public audience shapes the language of a formal written text.
answer: Context cannot be assumed, so the text must be explicit — low deixis, few unexplained references.
Interpretation cannot be checked in real time, so cohesion and structure must be strong.
The widest plausible audience is addressed, so specialised terms are defined or avoided.
Face needs of a diverse audience are managed through non-discriminatory language and hedging.

points.title: Features of formal writing
points.detail: Greater cohesion, editing, explicitness about context, complex syntax and nominalisation — and the capacity to be deliberately ambiguous.

questions.q: Identify four features of formal written language and explain what each signals.
answer: Standard English and careful editing — signals authority and credibility.

Nominalisation — raises formality and can remove the actor from the clause.
Specialised lexis or jargon — establishes expertise and assumes an informed reader.

points.title: Features of formal speech
points.detail: Formal speech carrying the organisational features of written language while still drawing on prosody and paralinguistic features; rehearsal and editing.

questions.q: Explain how a formal speech differs from both spontaneous speech and formal writing.
answer: Unlike spontaneous speech, it is rehearsed and edited, so non-fluency is minimal and structure is planned.
It carries written-language organisation: full clauses, clear sections, strong cohesion.
Unlike formal writing, it retains prosody and paralinguistics — pitch, stress, pause and gesture used deliberately for effect.
It sits between the two modes rather than belonging wholly to either.

points.title: Subsystem patterning and rhetoric
points.detail: Patterning across the subsystems used rhetorically — syntactic patterning such as antithesis, listing and parallelism, and phonological patterning.

questions.q: A speech includes: 'We have the resources. We have the expertise. We have the will.' Analyse the patterning used and its persuasive effect.
answer: Syntactic parallelism: three clauses of identical structure.
Repetition (anaphora) of 'We have the' at the start of each.
Tricolon: the three-part structure creates rhythm and a sense of completeness.
Effect: builds cumulative force, and the inclusive 'we' aligns speaker with audience, making the conclusion feel inevitable.

points.title: Jargon, euphemism, doublespeak and non-discriminatory language
points.detail: Jargon establishing expertise or excluding outsiders, euphemism negotiating taboo, doublespeak obscuring, and non-discriminatory language as a deliberate choice.

questions.q: Distinguish euphemism from doublespeak, and explain the different purposes each serves in public language.
answer: Euphemism substitutes a milder term for one considered harsh or taboo, usually to protect face.
Doublespeak deliberately obscures or reverses meaning to conceal an unwelcome reality.
Euphemism: 'passed away' for died — softening for the hearer's benefit.
Doublespeak: 'rightsizing' for mass redundancy — protecting the speaker, not the hearer.

points.title: Discourse strategies and cooperation in formal contexts
points.detail: How cooperation is managed when roles and turn-taking rights are unequal.

questions.q: Explain how politeness strategies are used to manage the power imbalance in a formal workplace email from an employee to a senior manager.
answer: Negative politeness dominates: hedging, modality and apology minimise imposition.
Indirect requests ('I was wondering whether') give the manager an easy refusal.
Formal address terms and full standard forms acknowledge the status difference.
The greater the social distance and power gap, the more mitigation is required.

Feature: modality and hedging ('it may be appropriate to consider') avoid direct imposition.
Expertise: jargon and specialised lexis signal membership of a professional field.

Modality 'may' and the minimiser 'a small number' reduce the apparent scale.
'Unauthorised access' is a euphemism for a data breach.
The text sits toward the obfuscation end of the clarify–manipulate–obfuscate range while appearing to disclose.

answer: Formal texts are planned and edited, so cohesive devices can be deliberately inserted.
The audience is unknown and absent, so links must be made explicit rather than inferred.
Conjunctive adverbials, clear reference chains and consistent lexical fields do the work that shared context does in conversation.
Informal speech relies on inference and deixis instead.

answer: SAE is codified in dictionaries, grammars and style guides and used by institutions — education, government, media.
Its status is social and historical, not a property of the variety itself.
Other varieties are systematic and rule-governed, with their own consistent patterns.
Calling them incorrect applies SAE's norms as a universal standard, which is prescriptivism.

Phonology: Australian vowels and non-rhoticity mark the speaker as local.
Discourse: understatement, self-deprecation and the levelling of status markers.

points.title: Broad, General and Cultivated accents
points.detail: The evolution of the three Australian accent groups, their phonological features, and the attitudes attached to each.

answer: Broad — strongest Australian features, historically associated with rural and working-class speakers.
General — the most widely used variety, occupying the middle of the continuum.
Cultivated — closest to Received Pronunciation, historically associated with prestige and education.
Cultivated has declined and now sometimes attracts negative judgement as affected, while Broad carries covert prestige as authentically Australian.

points.title: Cultural variation in Australian English
points.detail: How English varies according to culture — Standard Australian English, Aboriginal Australian Englishes and migrant ethnolects, and the features that mark each.

answer: Standard Australian English — codified, used in education, government and media.
Aboriginal Australian Englishes — a continuum drawing on First Nations languages, contact language and non-standard English features.
Migrant ethnolects — combine Australian English with features of a community's first language.
All three are systematic varieties; the differences are patterned, not random.

points.detail: Attitudes within Australian society to different varieties, including prescriptivist and descriptivist positions, and what those attitudes reveal about the holder.

answer: Prescriptivist — treating one variety as correct and change as decay.
Descriptivist response: language change is constant, systematic and observable in every period.
Features now considered standard were themselves once condemned as errors.
The task of linguistics is to describe how language is used, not to rule on how it should be.

answer: Borrowing and Americanisation: American lexis and spellings spread through media and software defaults.
Technology-driven innovation: new coinages and abbreviations originate online and move into speech.
Convergence: exposure to global varieties reduces some distinctly Australian features.
Speed of spread has increased — an innovation can be national within weeks rather than years.

answer: Shared lexis, accent and discourse conventions construct a recognisable national variety.
Certain features become emblematic — hypocoristics, understatement, the 'fair go' register of egalitarianism.
Contested because the identity constructed often reflects only some Australians.
It can exclude First Nations peoples and migrant communities whose varieties are equally Australian.

points.detail: Language features associated with emerging and established stereotypes, adopted consciously or subconsciously, and challenging the validity of those associations.

answer: This is a stereotype: a feature associated with a group and generalised to individuals.
Accent is not correlated with intelligence or education — it is a systematic phonological variety.
The judgement reflects overt prestige attached to more standard varieties, not linguistic fact.
Variation within any accent group exceeds the variation between groups, so the generalisation fails.

points.detail: Social and personal variation according to age, gender, sexuality, occupation, interests, aspirations and education.

answer: Sociolect: variation associated with a social group — age, occupation, interest, education, gender.
Idiolect: the unique combination of features used by one individual at a point in their life.
A person belongs simultaneously to groups defined by age, workplace, interests and region.
Their idiolect draws on all of these, and shifts as those group memberships change.

points.detail: How individual and group identities are represented across a range of written and spoken texts.

answer: Shared lexis — jargon, slang or in-group terms that only members fully interpret.
Discourse features — shared conventions for openings, humour, turn-taking and topic.
These construct the boundary of the group, marking who is inside and who is not.
Representation may be produced by the group itself, or imposed on it by outsiders through stereotype.

answer: Communities establish norms for register, taboo and politeness appropriate to each setting.
Individuals shift within their repertoire to meet the expectation — more formal register, less slang, more mitigation.
Breaching the norm carries social cost: loss of credibility, exclusion, or formal sanction.
Conforming earns acceptance and access to the group's resources.

answer: Repertoire is the range of varieties and registers a speaker can draw on.
In a job interview, shifting toward SAE and formal register claims overt prestige and institutional authority.
Among a peer group, using slang or a local variety claims covert prestige and signals solidarity.
A wider repertoire means more situations can be navigated successfully.

points.detail: Overt prestige attached to standard varieties and covert prestige attached to local forms, and how both can be deliberately used.

answer: Overt prestige attaches to the standard variety, recognised publicly and institutionally.
Covert prestige attaches to non-standard forms, valued within a group for signalling authenticity.
In a job interview the speaker shifts toward SAE, claiming overt prestige.
With friends afterwards they use slang and a broader accent, claiming covert prestige. Both are strategic uses of one repertoire.

Switches are typically rule-governed and occur at grammatically permissible points.
It is used purposefully — to signal group membership, express an idea unavailable in the other code, or include a listener.
Treating it as confusion applies a monolingual standard to multilingual competence.

'han(d)bag' — elision of /d/ in the consonant cluster.
Both suggest rapid, spontaneous, informal speech.
They indicate low planning and reduced social distance, not careless or incorrect speech.

'car' is /kaː/ rather than /kaːr/.

answer: Complex sentence — one main clause with two subordinate clauses.
Main clause: 'the committee accepted the submission'.
Subordinating conjunctions: 'Although' and 'because'.
A high density of subordination is a marker of formal written register.

'Although it rained, the match continued, and the crowd stayed.' — compound-complex; declarative.
'What time does it start?' — simple structure, interrogative type.

points.title: Word order
points.detail: Subject–verb–object, modifiers within a noun phrase, and the placement of adverbials — including what a departure from expected order achieves.

questions.q: A speaker says: 'Never in my life have I seen anything like it.' Identify the departure from standard word order and explain its effect.
answer: Fronting of the adverbial 'Never in my life', with subject–auxiliary inversion following.
Standard order would be 'I have never seen anything like it'.
The marked order foregrounds the adverbial, giving emphasis and heightening the emotional force.
It also raises the register — inversion of this kind is rare in casual speech.

points.title: Active and passive voice
points.detail: Including agentless passives, and why a writer might choose to remove the agent.

questions.q: A media release states: 'Errors were made in the processing of applications.' Identify the voice used, explain what the construction achieves, and rewrite it in the active voice.
answer: Agentless passive — 'were made' with no 'by' phrase identifying who made the errors.
It removes the actor, so responsibility is obscured while the error is acknowledged.
It also raises formality and depersonalises the statement.
Active: 'We made errors in processing applications' — or name the responsible party.

points.title: Syntactic patterning
points.detail: Antithesis, listing and parallelism, and the rhetorical effect each produces.

questions.q: A politician says: 'We were not elected to manage decline; we were elected to build.' Identify the syntactic patterning and explain its rhetorical effect.
answer: Antithesis — two contrasting ideas placed in a parallel grammatical structure.
Parallelism reinforces it: 'we were elected to...' repeated across both clauses.
The balance makes the contrast memorable and frames the second option as obviously preferable.
It also creates an in-group 'we' aligning speaker and audience.

answer: (2.0) — a timed pause of two seconds.
= — latching, where one turn follows immediately with no gap.
↗ — rising intonation on the following segment.

answer: 'It' — anaphoric reference back to 'the report'.
'However' — a conjunctive adverbial signalling contrast.
'these' — anaphoric reference to 'three changes'.
'The decision' — lexical cohesion, summarising the previous clause with a related noun.

points.area: Metalanguage by subsystem
points.title: Coherence
points.detail: Cohesion, inference, logical ordering, formatting, and consistency and conventions — and the difference between coherence and cohesion.

questions.q: Explain the difference between cohesion and coherence, and describe how a text could be cohesive but incoherent.
answer: Cohesion is the surface linking of a text through reference, conjunctions, ellipsis and lexical choice.
Coherence is whether the text makes sense as a whole to its reader.
A text can chain pronouns and conjunctions correctly while the ideas do not follow logically.
Coherence also depends on inference, logical ordering, formatting and conventions.

answer: Discourse markers: 'so', 'anyway'.
Non-fluency: a filled pause 'um', a pause (0.5), a false start and self-repair on 'the thing is—'.
Minimal response / backchannel: B's 'mm', signalling active listening without taking the floor.
Repetition of 'the thing is' is the repair completing the abandoned utterance.

Strategies are what speakers DO with those features to manage the interaction.

points.area: Metalanguage by subsystem
points.title: Politeness strategies
points.detail: Positive and negative face, positive and negative face-threatening acts, and positive and negative politeness.

questions.q: A colleague writes: 'Sorry to bother you — I don't suppose you'd have a moment to look at this, if you get a chance?' Identify the politeness strategies and explain which face need they address.
answer: Negative politeness — the writer avoids imposing.
Apology ('sorry to bother you'), hedging ('I don't suppose', 'if you get a chance') and modality ('would').
These address the reader's negative face: the want to be unimpeded and free from imposition.
The request is a face-threatening act, and the mitigation reduces the threat.

answer: They form a semantic domain (or lexical field) of food and cooking.
The domain establishes the field of the text and builds lexical cohesion.
It also signals the writer's expertise and assumes a reader who shares the register.

answer: Metaphor — households are described as drowning, mapping financial pressure onto physical danger.
It frames the situation as urgent and life-threatening rather than merely difficult.
The connotation positions the reader to view the budget negatively.

Antonymy: words of opposite meaning — 'increase' and 'decrease'.
Using related words across a text links sentences without repeating the same term.
This creates lexical cohesion and helps the reader follow the topic.

points.area: Metalanguage by subsystem
points.title: Euphemism and dysphemism
points.detail: Both as tools for negotiating taboo, and recognising that dysphemism can build solidarity as readily as it offends.

questions.q: Distinguish euphemism from dysphemism and explain how each can be used to negotiate taboo.
answer: Euphemism substitutes a milder expression for one felt to be harsh or taboo.
Dysphemism substitutes a harsher or more offensive expression than necessary.
Euphemism protects face and allows a taboo subject to be raised politely.
Dysphemism can build solidarity among intimates, or deliberately shock and offend — its effect depends on tenor.

questions.q: Define field, tenor and mode, and explain how each would differ between a text message to a friend and a letter from a bank.
answer: Field — the subject matter. Personal arrangements versus financial account information.
Tenor — the relationship between participants. Close and equal versus distant and institutionally unequal.
Mode — spoken or written and the degree of planning. Spontaneous written versus planned, edited written.
These situational factors drive the lexical, syntactic and discourse choices in each text.

Tenor is the relationship between participants, covering social distance and relative power.
Tenor is one of the situational factors that determines register.
A shift in tenor, such as a manager joining a conversation, produces a shift in register.

Metalinguistic: 'What do you mean by that?' — language used to talk about language itself.

points.title: Standard English, SAE, codification and standardisation
points.detail: What makes a variety standard, how codification works through dictionaries, style guides and grammars, and the prestige that follows.

questions.q: Explain what codification is and how it contributes to a variety becoming standard.
answer: Codification is the recording of a variety's forms in dictionaries, grammars and style guides.
It fixes spellings, meanings and conventions, giving an authority to appeal to.
Institutions then adopt the codified variety in education, government, law and media.
That institutional use, not any inherent quality, is what confers prestige on the variety.

points.title: Prescriptivism and descriptivism
points.detail: The two stances on language behaviour, and identifying which one a commentator is taking from their wording.

questions.q: Define prescriptivism and descriptivism, and identify which is at work in the statement 'Literally shouldn't be used for emphasis'.
answer: Prescriptivism: judging usage against rules of correctness and advocating how language should be used.
Descriptivism: observing and recording how language is actually used, without judgement.
The statement is prescriptivist — it rules on correct usage.
A descriptivist would note the intensifying use is widespread, patterned, and parallels earlier shifts such as 'really'.

answer: Positive face: the want to be liked, approved of and included.
Negative face: the want to be unimpeded and free from imposition.
Public correction threatens positive face — it damages the employee's standing in front of others.
Mitigation might include praise first, hedging, or correcting in private instead.

points.title: Overt and covert prestige
points.detail: Prestige attached to standard variants used by powerful groups, versus prestige attached to local forms that mark solidarity.

questions.q: Explain why covert prestige can lead a speaker to retain a stigmatised feature despite social pressure to drop it.
answer: Covert prestige is the value a non-standard form carries within a group.
Retaining it signals authenticity, loyalty and membership of that group.
Dropping it may be read as distancing yourself from your community.
The speaker weighs institutional advantage against group belonging — often keeping both varieties in their repertoire.

Sociolect — variation by social group, e.g. the lexis shared by medical professionals or by a teenage friendship group.
Idiolect — one individual's unique combination of features at a point in their life.
All three are systematic varieties, not deviations from a correct standard.

answer: Broad, General and Cultivated differ mainly in the realisation of vowels and diphthongs.
Broad has the most distinctly Australian realisations; Cultivated the closest to RP.
Speakers sit at points along a continuous scale, not in discrete boxes.
An individual may also shift along the continuum depending on context and audience.

They are rule-governed and systematic across all subsystems, with their own consistent patterns.

questions.q: Define code switching and distinguish it from register shifting.
answer: Code switching: moving between languages or distinct varieties within a single interaction.
Register shifting: moving between levels of formality within the same variety.
Code switching often signals group membership, identity or inclusion of a particular listener.
Both are strategic uses of a repertoire, but switching crosses varieties while shifting does not.

points.area: Linguistic terms and theories
points.title: Pidgin, creole and lingua franca
points.detail: A pidgin as nobody's first language, a creole as a pidgin that has become one, and a lingua franca as a shared language between groups.

questions.q: Distinguish between a pidgin, a creole and a lingua franca.
answer: A pidgin is a simplified contact variety that has no native speakers.
A creole is a pidgin that has acquired native speakers and developed full grammatical complexity.
A lingua franca is any shared language used between groups who do not share a first language.
The pidgin/creole distinction rests on native speakers, not on how simple the variety appears.

points.title: Language maintenance, shift and reclamation
points.detail: Resisting an encroaching language, switching to it, and the work of revitalising a language at risk of loss — with particular reference to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages.

questions.q: Distinguish between language maintenance, language shift and language reclamation, and identify which applies to efforts to revive an Aboriginal language with no remaining first-language speakers.
answer: Maintenance: a community continues using its language despite pressure from a dominant one.
Shift: the community progressively moves to the dominant language, often across generations.
Reclamation: reviving a language that has been lost or is at serious risk.
Reviving a language with no remaining first-language speakers is reclamation.

points.title: Slang, colloquial language, jargon and taboo
points.detail: The distinctions between them, since they are routinely confused, and swearing as a separate category again.

questions.q: Distinguish slang from colloquial language and from jargon, and explain why swearing is treated separately.
answer: Colloquial language is informal everyday language, widely understood across the speech community.
Slang is informal, group-specific and changes faster; it marks membership of a particular group.
Jargon is the specialised vocabulary of a field — precise for insiders, exclusionary for outsiders.
Swearing is a separate category because it can build solidarity and express emotion, not only cause offence.

points.title: Social distance and rapport
points.detail: The conceptual space between individuals or groups constructed by class, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, education, status and occupation — and rapport as agreement or sympathy between them.

questions.q: Explain what constructs social distance between participants, and describe two linguistic choices a speaker might make to reduce it.
answer: Social distance is constructed by class, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, education, status and occupation.
Choice: shifting to colloquial lexis, slang or hypocoristics to signal shared identity.
Choice: positive politeness — first names, inclusive 'we', agreement, in-group markers.
Reducing distance builds rapport; widening it asserts authority.

points.title: Multi-word lexemes and context-specific graphemes
points.detail: Sequences stored and retrieved as one unit, such as idioms and phrasal verbs; and written symbols whose meaning depends entirely on context.

questions.q: Define a multi-word lexeme and give two examples of different types.
answer: A sequence of words stored and retrieved as a single unit of meaning.
Idiom: 'kick the bucket' — meaning is not derivable from the individual words.
Phrasal verb: 'put up with'.
Also acceptable: compound nouns, fixed collocations.
